beats.voice_over: Imagine you are floating in cold, dark water. Twenty metres away, a black fin rises. Then another. Then five more.
beats.visual_plan: Underwater POV from the surface; black dorsal fins rising nearby. Low drone. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: You are now sharing the sea with the most successful predator on the planet.
beats.visual_plan: Orca pod passing, slow motion.

beats.voice_over: This animal hunts great white sharks and tears out their livers. It drowns blue whales, the largest animals that have ever lived. It makes waves to wash seals off the ice. It throws itself onto beaches to snatch sea lions from the shore.
beats.visual_plan: Quick cuts: shark silhouette, blue whale, ice floe, beach with sea lions (generic footage, no gore).

beats.voice_over: Nothing in the ocean is safe from it.
beats.visual_plan: Close-up of an orca eye. [1 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Except, it seems, you.
beats.visual_plan: Black screen. Music stops. [3 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: In the wild, across all of recorded history, there is not a single confirmed case of an orca killing a human.
beats.visual_plan: Text on screen: 0 CONFIRMED HUMAN DEATHS IN THE WILD. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: The ocean's deadliest predator refuses to treat us as prey. And the reason why may be one of the strangest stories in the animal kingdom.
beats.visual_plan: Title card: WHY ORCAS DON'T KILL HUMANS. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: To understand how strange that is, we first have to understand what an orca really is.
beats.visual_plan: Orca surfacing, mist from the blowhole.

beats.voice_over: The orca, or killer whale, is not really a whale in the way we usually picture one. It is the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family.
beats.visual_plan: Orcas and dolphins swimming (graphic family tree).

beats.voice_over: It can grow to nearly ten metres long and weigh up to ten tonnes. Females can live an estimated eighty to ninety years. Males, fifty to sixty.
beats.visual_plan: Size graphic: orca next to a diver and a bus.

beats.voice_over: Orcas live in every ocean on Earth, from the polar ice to the tropics. They hunt in coordinated family groups, and they have no natural predators at all.
beats.visual_plan: World map lighting up every ocean.

beats.voice_over: Scientists estimate that there are around fifty thousand orcas in the world's oceans. Fifty thousand of the most capable predators that have ever lived, sharing the sea with millions of swimmers, surfers, divers and fishermen every year.
beats.visual_plan: Busy beach and surfers seen from the water; an orca fin far offshore.

beats.voice_over: Fish, squid, seals, sea lions, dolphins, sharks, even the great whales. If it lives in the sea, some orca, somewhere, has learned to kill it.
beats.visual_plan: Montage of prey species.

beats.voice_over: A human swimmer is smaller, slower and weaker than almost everything on that list. By any logic, we should be easy prey.
beats.visual_plan: Lone swimmer seen from below, silhouetted against the surface. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: So before we try to answer the question, let's look at what orcas can do, when they decide something is food.
beats.visual_plan: Orca pod turning together. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: In the waters around the Antarctic Peninsula, scientists from the United States' National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration followed a group of orcas that hunt seals resting on floating ice.
beats.visual_plan: Antarctic pack ice, a seal on a floe.

beats.voice_over: First, they rise and look at the seal, heads above the surface. Then they back off, line up, and charge the floe together. Just before impact, they dive. The water they push forward keeps going, as a wave.
beats.visual_plan: Orcas spy-hopping; orcas swimming in formation; wave over ice.

beats.voice_over: If the seal holds on, they do it again. And again. And here is the detail that surprised everyone: Weddell seals made up only around fifteen percent of the seals on the ice, yet fourteen of the fifteen kills recorded were Weddell seals.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram: 15% → 14 of 15.

beats.voice_over: They were not taking whatever they found. They were choosing.
beats.visual_plan: Orca eye close-up. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: In Argentine Patagonia, some orcas ride a wave straight onto the beach, grab a sea lion pup, and twist back into the sea. It is extremely dangerous. An orca that misjudges the wave can end up stuck on the sand, where its own weight could kill it.
beats.visual_plan: Patagonian beach, sea lion colony, a tall fin offshore.

beats.voice_over: A local ranger reported that only seven orcas there were known to hunt this way, and only five of them taught it to younger whales. Young orcas follow an experienced hunter, stay close to the beach, and practise without fully committing.
beats.visual_plan: Young orca close to the shore, an adult nearby.

beats.voice_over: Off Western Australia, in 2019, researchers watched a dozen or so orcas chase down and kill a blue whale. Around fifty orcas then gathered to share it. By 2021, the same team had documented three blue whale kills in the area.
beats.visual_plan: Blue whale diving; many fins at the surface. Text: 3 BLUE WHALES.

beats.voice_over: And off South Africa, two male orcas named Port and Starboard drove great white sharks away from some of their favourite bays. In 2023, researchers watched Starboard, alone, kill a young great white in less than two minutes.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram of the two collapsed fins; dark shark silhouette.

beats.voice_over: Dead great whites washed up on the beaches, each missing the same organ: its liver, huge and rich in oil. On a single day in February 2023, at least seventeen sevengill sharks were found dead off the same coast, livers removed. In some places, shark cage diving, a whole local industry, came to a stop.
beats.visual_plan: Empty South African beach; shark cage diving boat at anchor.

beats.voice_over: These are not random attacks. They are techniques. Planned, practised, and passed down.
beats.visual_plan: Orca pod swimming in formation. [1 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: An animal that can hunt a great white shark could hunt a human in seconds. So why doesn't it?
beats.visual_plan: Swimmer silhouette from below; an orca shape passing far beneath. [3 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Let's look at the evidence. Every known encounter between wild orcas and people.
beats.visual_plan: Archive-style map with pins appearing.

beats.voice_over: In September 1972, near Point Sur in California, a surfer named Hans Kretschmer said he was bitten by an orca. He needed around a hundred stitches. Experts think it was a case of mistaken identity. He was wearing a black wetsuit, and sea lions were nearby.
beats.visual_plan: California coast, surfer in a black wetsuit on the water. Text: 1972.

beats.voice_over: The orca bit, and then let go. It did not come back.
beats.visual_plan: Calm water. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: In 1989, in Patagonia, researcher Bernd Würsig was standing near the water when a beaching orca surged towards him. It missed him by about a metre. He ran up the beach, unhurt.
beats.visual_plan: Pebble beach, wave rushing in. Text: 1989.

beats.voice_over: In August 2005, near Ketchikan in Alaska, a twelve-year-old boy named Ellis Miller was swimming in shallow water when a transient orca, one of the seal hunters, bumped him on the shoulder. Then it swam away. He was not bitten.
beats.visual_plan: Alaskan inlet, shallow water. Text: 2005.

beats.voice_over: In 2014, in New Zealand, a freediver was dragged underwater for more than forty seconds by an orca. But the orca had grabbed a bag tied to his arm, not the man. An expert called it an accidental entanglement.
beats.visual_plan: New Zealand estuary. Text: 2014.

beats.voice_over: Over many decades, that is about all the evidence there is. A handful of bites, bumps and close calls.
beats.visual_plan: Map with only a few pins.

beats.voice_over: The only death ever claimed is an old story from the Canadian Arctic, told by Inuit elders: a young man killed in the 1950s near orcas trapped in the ice. Researchers could never confirm it, and some think the cold water was the more likely cause.
beats.visual_plan: Arctic sea ice. Text: UNCONFIRMED. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Compare that with sharks. In 2025 alone, the International Shark Attack File recorded sixty-five unprovoked shark bites on people around the world, and nine deaths.
beats.visual_plan: Text: 2025 — 65 SHARK BITES, 9 DEATHS.

beats.voice_over: Orcas are bigger, smarter and better hunters than any shark. Some of them hunt sharks. And yet their record with us is almost empty.
beats.visual_plan: Split screen: shark silhouette / orca. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: But there is one place where that record looks very different.
beats.visual_plan: Concrete pool wall, empty and still. [3 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: In captivity, the story changes.
beats.visual_plan: Empty marine-park pool at night (generic, no logos). [1 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: There have been dozens of violent incidents between captive orcas and their trainers. And at least four people have died.
beats.visual_plan: Text on screen: CAPTIVITY: 4 DEATHS.

beats.voice_over: Three of those deaths involved a single male orca, Tilikum. The last was the SeaWorld trainer Dawn Brancheau, in 2010.
beats.visual_plan: Text: TILIKUM — 3 DEATHS. Slow push on dark water.

beats.voice_over: Researchers who study wild orcas point to what captivity takes away. In the wild, orcas swim dozens of kilometres every day with their families. In a tank, they have neither the space nor the social life they evolved for.
beats.visual_plan: Graphic: open ocean range vs a small rectangle.

beats.voice_over: The contrast is striking. Free orcas, with every opportunity, almost never hurt us. Confined orcas, under stress, sometimes do.
beats.visual_plan: Split screen: wild pod / empty tank. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: So whatever protects us in the wild, it is not that orcas are incapable of harming humans. It is something else. Something they bring with them from the open ocean.
beats.visual_plan: Wild pod swimming into blue water. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: And the first clue lies in what orcas choose to eat.
beats.visual_plan: Salmon swimming upstream. [2 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: In the 1970s, a Canadian scientist named Michael Bigg began studying the orcas off British Columbia, learning to recognise each whale by the shape of its dorsal fin.
beats.visual_plan: Pacific Northwest coastline, orcas surfacing.

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: He noticed something odd. In the very same waters, there were two kinds of orcas. And they did not mix.
beats.visual_plan: Two groups of orcas, one large, one small.

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: The first kind lived in large, tight family groups and ate fish, almost always salmon. Today they are known as residents.
beats.visual_plan: Large orca family group; salmon underwater.

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: The second kind roamed in smaller groups and ignored the salmon entirely. They hunted seals, sea lions and other whales. Today they carry his name: Bigg's killer whales.
beats.visual_plan: Small group of orcas; harbour seals on rocks.

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: Side by side, they look almost identical. But genetic studies suggest the two lines split more than three hundred thousand years ago. In 2024, a team of researchers even proposed that they are two separate species. The scientific community has not fully agreed.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram: resident vs Bigg's tree.

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: Here is what matters for us. Each orca population has its own menu, and it sticks to it. Whale researcher Erich Hoyt calls orcas fussy eaters. They eat what they learn to eat from their mothers and their families. Nothing more.
beats.visual_plan: Mother and calf swimming side by side.

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: A fish-eating resident orca does not suddenly decide to try a seal. And a seal-hunting orca has no tradition that says a human is food.
beats.visual_plan: Orca passing a seal without reacting (generic footage). [1 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: To an orca, food is not everything that moves. Food is what your family has always eaten.
beats.visual_plan: Orca family surfacing together. [2 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 6 — Theory one: we are not on the menu
beats.voice_over: And that knowledge has to come from somewhere. In orca society, it comes from the oldest females.
beats.visual_plan: Older female orca with a calf. [2 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: But wait. If orcas only harm what they eat, the story would be simple. It isn't.
beats.visual_plan: Harbour porpoise surfacing (Pixabay/Wikimedia). [1 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: The salmon-eating Southern Residents have a strange habit. They chase porpoises. They push them, toss them, sometimes for hours. And sometimes the porpoise dies.
beats.visual_plan: Orcas chasing a small porpoise at the surface (generic, no injury shown).

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: In 2023, a study led by Deborah Giles, of the research group Wild Orca, and Sarah Teman, of the University of California, Davis, reviewed more than sixty years of records. They found seventy-eight documented cases of Southern Residents harassing porpoises between 1962 and 2020.
beats.visual_plan: Text: 78 INCIDENTS, 1962–2020. MARINE MAMMAL SCIENCE.

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: They never eat them. Porpoises are not on their menu.
beats.visual_plan: Orca pod swimming away from a porpoise. [1 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: The researchers proposed three explanations. It could be social play that helps the group bond. It could be practice, with a porpoise standing in for a fast salmon. Or it could be a kind of misplaced caregiving, as if the orcas were trying to look after a small, weak animal.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram: PLAY / PRACTICE / MISPLACED CARE.

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: So orcas can harm animals they do not eat. Which makes their behaviour around people even more remarkable.
beats.visual_plan: Swimmer silhouette from below. [1 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 7 — A twist: killers that don't eat
beats.voice_over: Humans swim, surf, dive and sail in orca waters every day. And still, no wild orca has ever been confirmed to have killed one of us.
beats.visual_plan: Kayakers on a calm sea with fins in the distance. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Very few animals go through menopause. Humans do. And, as far as we know, only five other species do: all of them toothed whales. Orcas are one of them.
beats.visual_plan: Older female orca surfacing slowly.

beats.voice_over: A female orca stops having calves partway through her life. But she can live for decades afterwards.
beats.visual_plan: Graphic: timeline of a female's life.

beats.voice_over: Researchers from the University of Exeter found part of the answer by studying the resident orcas of the North Pacific over decades.
beats.visual_plan: Orca group travelling in a line.

beats.voice_over: When salmon are scarce, older post-menopausal females are more likely to lead the group as it travels and searches for food. They seem to carry the knowledge of where the fish can be found, built up over a lifetime of good years and bad ones.
beats.visual_plan: Lead orca in front of the pod; salmon run in a river.

beats.voice_over: In a 2019 study of almost four hundred young orcas, calves whose grandmother had died in the previous two years had a mortality rate four and a half times higher than calves with a living grandmother.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram: 4.5×.

beats.voice_over: In a society built on knowledge, the elders are the library. They teach where to hunt, how to hunt, and what to hunt.
beats.visual_plan: Grandmother, mother and calf swimming together.

beats.voice_over: And, perhaps, what to leave alone.
beats.visual_plan: Orca turning away into blue water. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Because if hunting traditions can be passed down for generations, so can the absence of one. No grandmother has ever taught her family that humans are prey.
beats.visual_plan: Slow push on the pod. [2 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: There may be another reason. Orcas are not just strong. They are careful.
beats.visual_plan: Orca gliding slowly close to a boat (generic).

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: They have one of the largest brains in the ocean, and they live in complex societies, with family bonds that can last a lifetime.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram: orca brain silhouette.

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: On July twenty-fourth, 2018, off the coast of British Columbia, a female resident orca known as Tahlequah, or J35, gave birth to a calf. The calf died within about half an hour.
beats.visual_plan: Calm grey sea, misty coastline.

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: She did not let go. She carried the body for about seventeen days, over roughly one thousand six hundred kilometres. Other members of her pod were seen taking turns.
beats.visual_plan: Counter: DAY 17. Orca surfacing slowly.

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: At the very end of 2024, she did it again. A new calf, a female, died within days, and Tahlequah was seen carrying her body into the new year.
beats.visual_plan: Grey winter sea, slow surfacing. [1 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: We cannot know what an orca feels. But an animal that behaves like this is not a simple hunting machine. It reacts to its world with something we struggle to name.
beats.visual_plan: Slow surfacing in soft light. [2 s — pause]

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: Hoyt says wild orcas are generally careful around people underwater.
beats.visual_plan: Orca passing a diver at a distance (generic, no contact).

beats.chapter: 9 — Theory three: an intelligent, careful animal
beats.voice_over: To an animal like this, a strange, slow, upright creature in the water may simply be something to investigate, not something to eat.
beats.visual_plan: Orca eye close-up, watching. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: For thousands of years, people along the coast of the North Pacific have lived alongside orcas. And some of their stories offer an answer of their own.
beats.visual_plan: Misty forest coastline of the Pacific Northwest.

beats.voice_over: One Tlingit story tells of Natsilane, a wood carver who was abandoned at sea by his own family. He carved a killer whale from wood, and it came to life and took revenge on those who betrayed him.
beats.visual_plan: Carved wooden orca (AI image), firelight.

beats.voice_over: Afterwards, Natsilane regretted the killing. And he told the whale that it must never harm a human again.
beats.visual_plan: Wooden orca dissolving into a real orca swimming. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: It is a legend, not science. But it says something people noticed long before scientists did: the ocean's greatest hunter seems to have an unwritten rule about us.
beats.visual_plan: Orca pod at dusk. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: And in the last few years, one group of orcas has put that rule to the test.
beats.visual_plan: Sailboat on the open sea. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Since 2020, sailors off the coasts of Spain and Portugal have reported a strange encounter. A group of orcas approaches a sailboat, goes straight for the rudder, and pushes, bites and spins it.
beats.visual_plan: Sailboat from above; rudder close-up.

beats.voice_over: More than seven hundred interactions have been logged. At least eight boats have sunk.

Online, the story became a revenge tale: orcas fighting back against humans. Most scientists studying them do not support that idea. Young orcas seem to copy the behaviour from older ones, the way a game spreads through a playground.
beats.visual_plan: Strait of Gibraltar from the air.

beats.voice_over: But look at what they target. The rudder. Not the people.
beats.visual_plan: Rudder close-up. [1 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Across hundreds of encounters, with crews standing on deck just a few metres away, no one has been injured by these orcas.
beats.visual_plan: Crew on a sailboat deck, calm sea. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Even when orcas develop a brand-new habit that involves humans, they still leave the humans alone.
beats.visual_plan: Orcas swimming away from the boat. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: So the answer to our question is not one thing. It is a combination. We are not on the menu. The elders never taught it. And orcas are careful, curious animals that rarely mistake us for anything they eat.
beats.visual_plan: Recap montage: salmon, grandmother, eye close-up, rudder.

beats.voice_over: But there is a darker side to this story. Because if anything in this relationship is dangerous, it is us.
beats.visual_plan: Industrial port, ships. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: The Southern Residents, a community of fish-eating orcas off Washington State and British Columbia, depend on Chinook salmon. And Chinook salmon have declined.
beats.visual_plan: Salish Sea, salmon run, dam.

beats.voice_over: In 1995, there were ninety-eight Southern Residents. By the end of 2021, there were seventy-three. The 2026 census counted seventy-six, and in October 2026, a new calf was spotted, bringing the count to seventy-seven.
beats.visual_plan: Diagram: 98 → 73 → 77.

beats.voice_over: The Iberian orcas, the ones spinning rudders, number fewer than fifty animals, and are considered critically endangered.
beats.visual_plan: Iberian coast.

beats.voice_over: The animals that refuse to hunt us are the ones that need our protection.
beats.visual_plan: Slow push on an orca surfacing at sunset. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: We gave them a frightening name: killer whale.
beats.visual_plan: Orca breaching in slow motion.

beats.voice_over: And they are killers. Perhaps the most skilled hunters in the ocean. They can take down a great white shark, a blue whale, a seal on the ice.
beats.visual_plan: Montage of the film's hunting shots.

beats.voice_over: But when they meet us, they look. They wonder. And they move on.
beats.visual_plan: Orca passing a boat, looking, then diving. [2 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: Not because they can't. But because, as far as we can tell, nothing in their culture tells them to.
beats.visual_plan: Orca family swimming into the sunset. [4 s — pause]

beats.voice_over: If you enjoyed this film, subscribe to Naturexplore for a new documentary every week. And tell us in the comments: why do you think orcas leave us alone?
beats.visual_plan: End card with two suggested videos.
